title: Thousands Rally in Israel Demanding Eisenkot‑Arab Deal to Oust Netanyahu – Al Jazeera Report
body:
Thousands of demonstrators flooded the streets of Tel Aviv on Saturday, calling on Israel’s opposition parties to forge a coalition with Arab lawmakers that could oust Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The massive rally, organized by a loose coalition of centrist and left‑wing groups, was framed as a “peaceful demand for a new political direction” after years of political deadlock, repeated elections and mounting public fatigue with the current government. While the crowd chanted slogans for change, a counter‑protest of Netanyahu supporters gathered nearby, warning that any alliance with Arab parties would empower “terrorists” and threaten Israel’s security.

The rally’s organizers emphasized that a partnership with Arab parties is not a concession to extremist agendas but a pragmatic step toward breaking the stalemate that has plagued Israeli politics since 2021. Since the last parliamentary election, Israel has held four votes for a government, each ending in a deadlock that forced the country into a series of short‑lived caretaker administrations. The latest poll numbers show Netanyahu’s Likud party trailing behind a bloc of centrist and left‑leaning parties that together command a slim majority if they can secure the support of the Arab‑Israeli parties, primarily Ra’am (United Arab List) and the Joint List. Proponents argue that such a coalition would bring much‑needed stability, enable the passage of a 2025 budget, and restore confidence among investors and international partners.

Opponents, however, remain deeply skeptical. Netanyahu’s right‑wing base, still energized by his hard‑line stance on security and settlement expansion, views any collaboration with Arab parties as an existential threat. The counter‑demonstration, which featured banners reading “No Terrorists in Government” and “Netanyahu Is Our Only Shield,” reflected a broader narrative that equates Arab political participation with delegitimization of the Jewish state. This rhetoric has been amplified by several right‑wing Knesset members who warn that granting Arab parties ministerial influence could embolden Hamas and other militant groups, especially amid the ongoing Gaza conflict that has inflamed public sentiment.

Analysts note that the prospect of an Eisenkot‑Arab coalition—named after veteran politician Yair Eisenkot, who has been floated as a potential compromise figure—faces both logistical and ideological hurdles. Eisenkot, a former defense minister, enjoys a reputation for security expertise but has never led a party, raising questions about his ability to command a unified front. Moreover, the Arab parties themselves are divided: while Ra’am has previously entered a historic coalition with right‑wing Prime Minister Naftali Bennett in 2021, its leadership now insists on concrete guarantees for Palestinian rights, an agenda that could clash with the security priorities of any centrist partner. The internal dynamics of these parties, coupled with the deep mistrust on both sides, make the formation of a stable government a delicate balancing act.

International observers are watching the developments closely. The United States and European Union have repeatedly urged Israel to pursue a more inclusive political framework, arguing that broad representation could ease regional tensions and improve prospects for a negotiated peace. Meanwhile, regional actors such as Jordan and Egypt have signaled tentative support for any Israeli government that demonstrates a willingness to engage with Arab constituents, seeing it as a possible conduit for renewed diplomatic dialogue. Yet, the volatile security environment—marked by periodic flare‑ups along the Gaza border and the ever‑present threat of rocket attacks—means that any coalition will be tested almost immediately after its formation.

As Israel heads toward another election cycle, the outcome of Saturday’s rally may serve as a barometer for public appetite for change. If the opposition can translate street momentum into a viable parliamentary agreement, the country could see its first government that includes Arab parties in a meaningful role, potentially reshaping domestic policy and foreign relations. Conversely, if the counter‑protest narrative prevails, Netanyahu’s Likud may retain its grip, perpetuating the cycle of elections and political uncertainty. The coming weeks will reveal whether Israel’s electorate is ready to embrace a new coalition model or will continue to cling to entrenched divisions, a decision that will shape the nation’s trajectory for years to come.
